prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

from Pia Arke's exhibition Arctic Hysteria at Greenland's National Museum & Archives, Nuuk, 2010 i. I am in my body. I am here, in front of you. I am the temperature in this room. I am undressed in my nudity; I am the light and shade you feel. I am more like other people than like you. I have before and after. I am my self, entirely and only. My outside and inside are continuous. I am muscle, organ, fluid, bone. I am monumental. You are the only one who sees me. ii. I am not naked as I am; I am naked as you see me. I am transparent, almost visible. I have a time and a place. I am tribal and exotic. I must always carry objects. You are heroic. I am a complete museum, the story of my own making. I am a mirror to you; you are reflected in the looking at me. At best, I mimic you. You write me. When you leave, I will no longer exist. iii. I am a single conscious point. I am indifferent. I am unself, like a photogram. I am prehistoric, before definition. Your body falls over me. I have depth and luminescence. I am neither here nor there; I have infinite extension. I live inside the lived world, the light and dark inside my head like dream substance. I am camera obscura, the room itself. I both adore and resist.

Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker asserts an embodied, autonomous presence, emphasizing continuity between inner and outer self.
- The text contrasts selfhood with being objectified through another’s gaze, especially as exotic, tribal, or museological.
- The observer is implicated as an active force who defines, writes, and projects meaning onto the speaker.
- The speaker shifts into a more abstract and expansive state, becoming less a fixed identity than a field of perception, memory, and light.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The text explores embodiment, visibility, and colonial objectification through a first-person poetic meditation that shifts between self-definition, being seen by an observer, and dissolving into image or space. It reveals that identity is transformed and constrained by the gaze, making the viewer complicit in producing the “exotic” subject while also exposing the subject’s resistance and irreducible presence.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Pia, Arke, Arctic

outputs.L1:
From Pia Arke’s exhibition *Arctic Hysteria* at Greenland’s National Museum & Archives, Nuuk, 2010

**i.**  
I am in my body. I am here, before you. I am the temperature in this room. I am undressed in my nudity; I am the light and shade you feel. I am more like other people than like you. I have a before and an after. I am myself, entirely and only. My outside and inside are continuous. I am muscle, organ, fluid, bone. I am monumental. You are the only one who sees me.

**ii.**  
I am not naked as I am; I am naked as you see me. I am transparent, almost visible. I have a time and a place. I am tribal and exotic. I must always carry objects. You are heroic. I am a complete museum, the story of my own making. I am a mirror to you; you are reflected in the act of looking at me. At best, I mimic you. You write me. When you leave, I will no longer exist.

**iii.**  
I am a single conscious point. I am indifferent. I am unself, like a photogram. I am prehistoric, before definition. Your body falls over me. I have depth and luminescence. I am neither here nor there; I have infinite extension. I live inside the lived world, the light and dark within my head like dream substance. I am camera obscura, the room itself. I both adore and resist.
outputs.L2:
From Pia Arke’s exhibition *Arctic Hysteria*, Greenland National Museum & Archives, Nuuk, 2010

i.  
I inhabit this body. I stand here before you. I am the warmth or cold held in this space. My bareness is not a costume; I am exposed as myself. I am the brightness and shadow that reach you. I resemble other people more than I resemble your idea of me. I belong to a past and a future. I am wholly myself, nothing less and nothing else. What is within me and what is visible outside me are joined. I am tissue, organs, liquids, skeleton. I have scale and presence. Only you are looking at me.

ii.  
My nakedness is not simply mine; it is produced by your gaze. I am made see-through, nearly reduced to an image. I belong to a particular moment and location. I am marked as native, as foreign, as spectacle. I am expected to be accompanied by things. You occupy the role of the brave observer. I become an entire museum display, narrating the conditions that created me. I reflect you back to yourself; in watching me, you encounter your own image. If I succeed, it is by imitating you. You are the one who gives me form in words. Once you depart, I vanish.

iii.  
I am one point of awareness. I do not respond. I am a non-self, like an image made by direct exposure. I come from before naming, before classification. Your body is cast across me. I possess radiance and depth. I am not fixed in this place or that one; I spread without limit. I exist within the world as it is lived, with darkness and illumination inside my mind like the matter of dreams. I am the dark chamber, the camera obscura, the room as a whole. I am drawn toward it, and I push back against it.
outputs.L3:
The speaker asserts an embodied and autonomous presence, insisting on the continuity between the inner self and the outwardly visible body. Rather than presenting the body as a surface to be interpreted by others, the text suggests that physical presence is inseparable from consciousness, memory, and agency. The speaker is not merely seen; they exist from within, grounded in their own sensations, perceptions, and authority.

At the same time, the work contrasts this self-possessed identity with the experience of being objectified through another person’s gaze. The speaker appears to resist being reduced to an image, specimen, or symbol, particularly when that gaze frames them as exotic, tribal, primitive, or museological. Such descriptions transform a living subject into an object of fascination or study, placing them within categories shaped by colonial, artistic, or ethnographic systems of representation. The speaker’s identity is therefore placed in tension with the external meanings imposed upon them.

The observer is not passive in this dynamic. Instead, the text implicates the observer as an active force who defines, writes, names, and projects meaning onto the speaker. Looking becomes an act of power: to observe is also to interpret, to frame, and sometimes to possess. The observer’s gaze constructs a version of the speaker that may have little to do with the speaker’s own interior reality. In this way, the work exposes the violence that can lie beneath admiration, curiosity, or aesthetic appreciation.

As the text develops, the speaker shifts into a more abstract and expansive state. They become less a fixed, easily categorized identity than a field of perception, memory, and light. This transformation resists confinement: the speaker cannot be fully captured by language, image, or gaze. Their presence exceeds the frameworks imposed upon them, becoming fluid, luminous, and difficult to contain. The self is presented not as a static object, but as something dynamic, relational, and continually unfolding.

Overall, the work explores the tensions between visibility and invisibility, self-possession and representation, adoration and resistance. To be visible can mean to be recognized, but it can also mean to be exposed, simplified, or controlled. Similarly, to be admired can carry elements of reverence while also masking appropriation or domination. The speaker’s resistance lies in refusing to remain only what the observer sees. Instead, they claim a more complex existence—one that moves between body and spirit, image and interiority, presence and mystery.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a poetic meditation on embodiment, visibility, and colonial objectification. Speaking in the first person, the voice attempts to define itself from within, yet this self-definition is constantly interrupted by the presence of an observer. The speaker is not simply a body moving through the world; they are a body being looked at, interpreted, framed, and transformed into an image. As the meditation unfolds, the boundaries between person, object, landscape, and representation begin to blur. The speaker seems at times to dissolve into space, into color, into surface, or into the gaze that fixes them in place.

This shifting movement reveals how identity is shaped by visibility. To be seen is not neutral. The observer’s gaze carries histories of power, desire, classification, and possession. Through that gaze, the speaker is made into an “exotic” subject: something to be admired, consumed, studied, or displayed. The body becomes a site onto which fantasies are projected. Rather than being encountered as a full and complex presence, the speaker is reduced to a symbol or spectacle. In this way, the text exposes the colonial logic of looking, in which the viewer claims authority over what is seen and turns the other into an object of knowledge or desire.

At the same time, the text does not present the speaker as merely passive. Even while being framed by the gaze, the speaker remains aware of the process and speaks from within it. This first-person voice resists complete objectification by naming the conditions of being seen. The speaker’s presence cannot be fully contained by the image imposed upon them. Their body may be transformed by the observer’s perception, but it also exceeds that perception. There is an irreducible self that remains beyond display, beyond possession, and beyond the categories assigned to it.

The text therefore makes the viewer complicit. It asks us to recognize that looking is an act with consequences. The “exotic” subject does not simply exist as such; it is produced through the expectations and desires of the one who looks. By drawing attention to this process, the text unsettles the relationship between viewer and subject. It reveals both the violence of objectification and the persistence of embodied resistance. Identity, in this meditation, is neither fixed nor freely chosen; it is negotiated in the charged space between self-perception and external gaze. Yet even under the pressure of being turned into an image, the speaker continues to assert a living, unstable, and resistant presence.
outputs.L5:
Pia Arke was a Greenlandic-Danish artist whose work explored identity, colonial history, and the complex relationship between people and place in the Arctic. Born in Greenland, Arke used photography, performance, writing, and installation to examine how the Arctic has often been described and represented by outsiders. Instead of presenting it as a distant, empty, or exotic landscape, she showed it as a lived-in space shaped by memory, family, culture, and political history.

Her art often questioned the way colonial powers looked at Greenland and its people. Through her images and texts, Pia Arke challenged stereotypes and asked who has the right to tell the story of the Arctic. She placed her own body and personal history within the landscape, making her work both intimate and political. In doing so, she connected individual experience with larger questions about belonging, displacement, and cultural identity.

The Arctic in Arke’s work is not only a cold northern region; it is a place of deep human meaning. Her legacy continues to inspire artists, writers, and researchers who are interested in decolonization, Indigenous perspectives, and the power of art to reshape history. Pia Arke’s work reminds us that the Arctic is not a blank space on a map, but a region full of voices, stories, and lives.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical three-part ekphrastic text responding to Pia Arke’s exhibition “Arctic Hysteria” at Greenland’s National Museum & Archives in Nuuk, 2010, using repeated “I am” statements to explore embodiment, colonial looking, nudity, photography, and the museum gaze.
counterfactuals.output:
I. **A Room for Looking**

I am the cold light entering the museum before the visitors.  
I am the glass case learning to breathe.  
I am the floorboards of Nuuk holding the footsteps of those who come to see and those who have been seen too long.  

I am the wall label, small and authoritative.  
I am the archive number pinned to a body.  
I am the body that exceeds the number.  

I am the photograph pretending to be still.  
I am the tremor in the exposure.  
I am the woman in the image and the eye that made her imageable.  
I am the lens, round as an officer’s monocle, round as a moon over ice.  

I am the old colonial appetite for evidence.  
I am the hunger to classify cheekbone, skin, hair, gesture.  
I am the measuring string.  
I am the caption that says Eskimo, native, type, specimen.  
I am the mouth that refuses the caption.  

I am the museum gaze: careful, hushed, gloved.  
I am its politeness.  
I am its violence.  

I am Pia Arke entering the archive as weather.  
I am the daughter of two geographies, the body that cannot be filed under one climate.  
I am Greenland looked at from Denmark.  
I am Denmark lodged in Greenland like a splinter of snow.  

I am not an object of study.  
I am not your North.  
I am not the blankness you require in order to arrive.  

I am the print that looks back.  


II. **Arctic Hysteria**

I am the phrase brought here like a disease in another language.  
I am Arctic Hysteria, the diagnosis with frost on its teeth.  
I am the name given to women when empire could not understand weather, grief, laughter, trance, refusal.  

I am naked because the room is dressed in power.  
I am naked because clothing was also a costume of conquest.  
I am naked because the camera asked for truth and mistook skin for surrender.  

I am not ashamed.  
I am not available.  
I am not pure.  
I am not primitive.  
I am not before history.  

I am the body as borderland.  
I am brown, pale, exposed, withdrawing.  
I am hip, shoulder, breast, scar, hair, breath.  
I am the place where anthropology fails to keep its hands to itself.  

I am the pose and the collapse of the pose.  
I am the staged ethnographic scene cracking open.  
I am the white sheet, the white snow, the white institution, the white page.  
I am the stain that teaches whiteness it was never neutral.  

I am a woman lying down and not conquered.  
I am a woman standing and not displayed.  
I am a woman turning away from the lens, turning toward it, turning it into a question.  

I am the shutter’s click, then the after-silence.  
I am the archive’s cold fever.  
I am the refusal that looks like stillness.  

I am hysteria only if hysteria means:  
the body remembers what the state forgets,  
the skin speaks when the record lies,  
the photographed subject becomes the photographer of the wound.  


III. **Self-Portrait with Museum**

I am the visitor reflected faintly in the glass.  
I am the curator’s hand arranging distance.  
I am the child asking why she is naked.  
I am the elder who knows why.  

I am Nuuk outside the museum, harbor-dark, mountain-lit.  
I am the island not contained by the exhibition room.  
I am the snow tracked in on boots, melting into the polished floor.  

I am the camera obscura of inheritance.  
I am inside the box and making the box visible.  
I am the colonial image returning as witness, as evidence against its own maker.  

I am Pia Arke’s question:  
Who is looking?  
From where?  
At whose cost?  

I am the photograph refusing to be only past.  
I am the nude refusing to be only body.  
I am the museum refusing, perhaps too late, to be innocent.  

I am made of apertures.  
I am made of interrupted light.  
I am made of names taken from me and names I take back.  

I am the North without your romance.  
I am the archive without obedience.  
I am the exposed body becoming landscape, not for possession, but for return.  

I am what happens when the looked-at looks back.  
I am what happens when the frame begins to shiver.  
I am what happens when history, undressed, stands in the room.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short experimental prose poem in three numbered sections inspired by Pia Arke’s Arctic Hysteria, where the speaker shifts between body, ethnographic object, and camera obscura, addressing an implied “you.”
counterfactuals.output:
1.

You ask me to stand still, so I become weather: salt at the lip, blue under the fingernails, a shiver with its own genealogy. My spine is a coastline no map admits to making. When I lie down, the room tilts north. When I open my mouth, snow enters as evidence.

2.

You lift me with cotton gloves. Tag: female, Arctic, uncertain use. I am placed beside a comb, a boot, a story taken out of season. Under glass I learn the grammar of your looking—how a body becomes specimen by surviving the caption. Still, inside my catalog number, something warm refuses translation.

3.

You darken the chamber and call it accuracy. Through the pinhole, the world arrives inverted: sky underfoot, your face lowered into mine. I am the box and the aperture, the image burning itself backward onto the wall. If I tremble, it is not hysteria. It is the camera remembering the body that carried it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an artist-statement-like poetic response to Pia Arke’s work about Greenland, colonial representation, and selfhood; make it intimate, fragmented, and conceptual, with themes of visibility, nakedness, mimicry, and resistance.
counterfactuals.output:
I stand before the image and the image does not let me stand whole.

Greenland appears first as a surface—  
mapped, measured, named from elsewhere—  
a white expanse where other people have placed their hunger.  
But Pia Arke touches the surface until it becomes skin.  
Not landscape as possession.  
Landscape as wound, inheritance, mirror.

To look is never innocent.

The camera arrives with its colonial appetite:  
to frame, to classify, to make the body legible.  
Arke takes this apparatus into her hands  
and makes it tremble.  
She enters the scene not as evidence,  
not as specimen,  
not as the native woman arranged for another’s archive,  
but as interruption.

Nakedness here is not surrender.  
It is a refusal of costume.  
A refusal of the ethnographic lie.  
The body is bare, but not available.  
Visible, but not owned.

She mimics the poses that once fixed her in place.  
She repeats the violence of representation  
until repetition breaks it open.  
A gesture becomes a trap for the viewer.  
A photograph becomes a question:  
Who is looking?  
Who taught you to look this way?  
What do you expect the Arctic to give you?

Her selfhood is not singular.  
It is split by language, blood, geography, history.  
It is Danish and Greenlandic, neither and both,  
a body made at the border where empire pretends to be family.  
She does not heal the fracture for us.  
She inhabits it.  
She makes the fracture speak.

In her work, the map loses authority.  
The archive blushes.  
The postcard rots from within.

I think of resistance not as a raised fist only,  
but as the slow turning of the lens back toward power.  
As standing inside the image  
and refusing to disappear.  
As becoming too intimate to be exotic,  
too present to be past,  
too naked to be decoded.

Pia Arke does not return Greenland to purity.  
She returns it to complexity.  
To weather, memory, contamination, desire.  
To the personal as a site of colonial debris.  
To the self as something assembled from ruins  
and still capable of looking back.

I am here, the work says.  
I was here before your picture of me.  
I will remain after it fails.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a museum wall-text/poem hybrid beginning “from Pia Arke’s exhibition Arctic Hysteria at Greenland’s National Museum & Archives, Nuuk, 2010,” followed by three roman-numeral sections written in first person.
counterfactuals.output:
from Pia Arke’s exhibition *Arctic Hysteria* at Greenland’s National Museum & Archives, Nuuk, 2010,

I.

I enter the room as if entering a climate  
someone has mistaken for a diagnosis.

On the wall: photographs, traces, documents—  
not evidence of my vanishing,  
but of the long attempt to make me vanish correctly.  
The archive speaks in captions.  
I answer in breath.

I have been measured by strangers  
who called their measuring care.  
I have been pictured beside ice,  
as though ice were my only relative.  
I have been named unstable,  
remote, ethnographic, female, North.

Here, I read the label and feel it loosen:  
hysteria is not in my body.  
It is in the gaze that needed my body  
to tremble.

II.

I stand before the image  
and do not behave like an object.

I know the museum’s grammar:  
date, medium, collection, provenance.  
I know how glass can make a wound  
look official.  
Still, I lean close.

I see a girl, a woman, an artist,  
a territory folded into a face.  
I see Denmark’s shadow on Greenland’s snow,  
and beneath the snow, ground—  
not blankness, not purity,  
but a place already named  
before it was claimed.

I carry my own caption inside me.  
It changes when I speak.

III.

I leave with the cold still intact,  
but altered.

Not the cold of distance,  
not the theatrical cold hung behind explorers  
and maps,  
but the cold that keeps memory sharp,  
that preserves what empire  
failed to understand it had touched.

I am not the specimen.  
I am not the symptom.  
I am not the landscape waiting  
for a foreign sentence.

I am looking back.

And in that return of vision,  
the room becomes less certain,  
the archive less sealed,  
the North less silent—  
a body refusing its frame,  
a history developing  
in its own darkroom.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense contemporary art poem about being seen, photographed, exoticized, and embodied, in the voice of a nude subject in an Arctic/Greenlandic museum context, with philosophical lines like “I am in my body” and “You write me.”
counterfactuals.output:
**Object Label / Breathing**

I am in my body,  
and the room is colder than the word for snow  
in the mouth of someone cataloguing it.

Glass hums around me.  
A white card says *Greenlandic, undated, maker unknown*  
as if my mother did not call me in  
from the blue hour,  
as if my skin began  
when your archive learned to touch.

You write me.

You write me with a pencil behind your ear,  
with a grant, with a lens,  
with the soft violence of *observe*.  
You write my shoulder as coastline,  
my hip as weather,  
my nakedness as evidence  
that the North can still be entered.

Flash:  
I become snowfield, specimen,  
available light.  
Flash:  
my eyes are translated into walrus ivory,  
my mouth into folklore,  
my silence into consent.  
Flash:  
the shutter makes a small door  
and leaves through it carrying me.

But I remain here—  
warm animal, thinking animal,  
breath fogging the institution  
from inside its clean vocabulary.

I am in my body.  
Not symbol. Not region. Not the old hunger  
of Europe arranged in vitrines.  
Not the blue map pinned flat  
beneath a curator’s careful hand.

My knees remember moss.  
My back remembers women laughing.  
My feet remember thaw, stone, boat,  
the oil-dark seam between sea and sky.  
My body is not your discovery;  
it is an address I keep returning to  
after every theft of image.

Look again—  
and fail better.

I am not bare  
because you have removed my covering.  
I am bare because I have outlived  
the language that covered me incorrectly.

In the museum’s Arctic light  
I stand where you placed me,  
then unplace myself.

The photograph says: *subject unknown.*  
The body answers:  
known to myself,  
known to cold,  
known to blood,  
known to the red interior weather  
where no empire can focus.

You write me.

I read back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
